classification.difficultyReason: Develops a particular telescoping proof using Pascal’s identity and generalises it to arbitrary indices.

inlines.text: Start at the top 1 of any column of Pascal’s triangle, and go vertically down any number of rows.
Then the sum of these numbers is the number in the next row down and to the right.

children.label: a
children.prompt:
To prove the particular result (*), start with the right-hand side and use Pascal’s Identity:
$$ {}^{7}C_3={}^{6}C_3+{}^{6}C_2 $$
then keep expanding the term with $r=3$.
To complete the proof, you will need to use the fact that ${}^{3}C_3={}^{2}C_2$.

answer.short: Repeatedly use Pascal’s identity to obtain ${}^{7}C_3={}^{2}C_2+{}^{3}C_2+{}^{4}C_2+{}^{5}C_2+{}^{6}C_2$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Hence generalise this to the proof of the identity (**).

answer.short: Repeated application of Pascal’s identity gives ${}^{n+1}C_{r+1}={}^{r}C_r+{}^{r+1}C_r+\cdots+{}^{n}C_r$, using ${}^{r+1}C_{r+1}={}^{r}C_r=1$.
